name: Lethal means safety counseling (CALM-informed)
evidenceLevel: Emerging evidence for the counseling itself. In a factorial RCT with 232 firearm-owning National Guard members, a brief, motivational interviewing-informed lethal means counseling session increased safe firearm storage at 3 months compared with control (55% vs 39%); suicide outcomes were not measured (Anestis et al., 2021). A Military Health System review notes that lethal means counseling improved safe storage of medicines and firearms but that its effect on suicide outcomes is unknown. The 2024 VA/DoD suicide risk guideline stresses means safety at every step of care, suggests assessing access to firearms, and found weak evidence for population-level means-reduction efforts. CALM (Counseling on Access to Lethal Means) is a free SPRC course listed in SPRC's Best Practices Registry.
purpose: Many suicidal crises are brief, and the method within reach in that moment matters, because some methods, especially firearms, are more likely to be fatal. Lethal means counseling is a collaborative conversation with the client, and with consent their family or household, about temporarily putting time and distance between a person at risk and the most dangerous means, especially firearms and stockpiled medicines. It respects the client's values (including firearm ownership) and focuses on safety during a high-risk period, not on permanent removal or politics. Based on the principles taught in CALM; the wording here is original.
steps: Ask every client who has suicidal thoughts, in a matter-of-fact way, about access to firearms (at home, in vehicles, at other people's homes) and to medicines (including saved-up supplies), plus any other means they mention.
Explain the reason in plain language: crises often pass, and putting time and distance between a person and a lethal method can save a life.

Explore options with the client, respecting their values. For firearms: temporary storage away from home with a trusted person, or at a gun shop, range or law-enforcement agency where legal; or, as a next-best step, locked storage with someone else holding the key or code and ammunition kept separately. For medicines: dispose of medicines no longer needed, keep only small amounts at home, and have someone else hold the rest.
With consent, involve a family member or support person and agree on who will do what, and by when.
Check local laws on transferring firearms and on extreme risk protection orders. Point to legal resources rather than giving legal advice.
Add the agreed steps to the safety plan (safety-plan handout), and agree how and when firearms or medicines will be returned once risk is lower.
Follow up at the next contact to confirm the steps were taken, and problem-solve any barriers.
Before using this routinely, complete training such as the free CALM course.
script: I ask everyone who is going through a hard time about this. Are there guns in your home, or anywhere you can easily get to them?
This isn't about taking anything away for good. It's about putting some time and distance between you and the most dangerous things while you're going through a rough patch.
Most suicidal crises pass. Having a gun or a lot of pills nearby makes a bad moment much more dangerous.
Is there someone you trust who could hold on to your firearms for a while? Or could someone else keep the key?
What about medicines? Could we get rid of old ones and have someone hold the extras?
Would it be okay to bring your partner or a family member into this plan?
When things are better, we can plan how and when things come back.
contraindications: This conversation supports, but does not replace, suicide risk assessment and clinical decisions about level of care. This tool does not judge risk. If risk appears imminent, follow emergency procedures: in the US, call or text 988 or call the local emergency number; elsewhere, use the local emergency number or findahelpline.com.
Do not ask a family member to remove firearms if doing so could provoke violence. Consider domestic violence risk, and involve legal resources or law enforcement where appropriate.
Firearm transfer and storage laws vary by state and country. Do not give legal advice; point to local legal resources.
A confrontational or political tone can damage trust. Lead with shared concern for safety and respect for the client's values.
Medicines: do not advise stopping prescribed medicines. Coordinate with the prescriber or pharmacist about smaller supplies or other safer dispensing options.

Alcohol raises risk in a crisis. Include plans to reduce access to alcohol where relevant. Do not enter identifying details into this tool; nothing is stored or sent. Any note or export about substance use must carry this notice: 42 CFR Part 2 prohibits unauthorized disclosure of these records.
culturalAdaptations: Firearm ownership can be tied to identity, work, personal safety, hunting and rural life. Respect this, and frame storage as temporary and as protecting the client and their family.
In rural areas, distance to storage sites can be a barrier. Problem-solve with options that are actually available locally.
Veterans and service members may respond to peer-based framing ('looking out for each other'). VA and Military Health System resources support this approach.
For clients who distrust police or government, do not suggest law-enforcement storage first; offer trusted private options.
Medicines may be shared within families or kept as traditional remedies. Ask respectfully about everything in the home.
